common_name: Viking Birdsfoot Trefoil (Standard Broad-Leaved Pasture & Cover Legume)

planting.note: Sow shallowly into a firm, weed-free seedbed in spring using fresh seed inoculated with Lotus-specific Rhizobium; Viking is an older broad-leaved trefoil type long used as a benchmark cultivar in regional variety trials.

directions: Viking is a standard broad-leaved birdsfoot trefoil cultivar that has served for decades as a comparison check in forage variety trials across the northern US and Canada. Like other trefoils it establishes slowly and competes poorly with weeds as a seedling, so mow or clip the stand in its first season to keep weed pressure down while the taproot develops. Once established it tolerates wet, acidic, or infertile soils that stress alfalfa and clover, fixing nitrogen and providing non-bloating grazing or hay for several years without reseeding. Use certified inoculant at seeding since naturalized Lotus-specific rhizobia are often absent from fields with no trefoil history.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Birdsfoot Trefoil

common_name: AU Dewey Birdsfoot Trefoil (High-Tannin Bloat-Safe Forage Legume)

planting.note: Drill shallowly into a firm, weed-free seedbed in spring with fresh, inoculated seed; AU Dewey was bred at Auburn University for the humid, acidic soils of the lower South where most other trefoil cultivars struggle.

directions: AU Dewey is a birdsfoot trefoil cultivar developed at Auburn University and selected for elevated condensed-tannin content, which makes trefoil forage naturally bloat-safe for grazing cattle unlike alfalfa or clover. It was bred specifically for adaptation to the acidic, poorly drained soils typical of the Southeast, where older northern trefoil cultivars often fail to persist. Seedlings establish slowly and need weed suppression by mowing during the first growing season, after which the stand provides season-long, non-bloating grazing. Maintain near-neutral surface pH where possible and avoid close, continuous grazing that depletes taproot reserves before the plant can set seed and reseed naturally.
sources: Auburn University Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Birdsfoot Trefoil

planting.note: Drill seed-in-pod shallowly into firm, well-drained, calcareous ground in early spring or late summer; Mountainview was bred in Canada specifically for seeding in mixtures with alfalfa to reduce pasture bloat risk.

directions: Mountainview is a Canadian sainfoin cultivar developed for grazing in mixed stands with alfalfa, where its condensed tannins help offset the bloat risk that pure alfalfa pastures carry. It forms a deep, taprooted perennial crown that fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis and draws on subsoil moisture, giving it strong drought tolerance once established on well-drained, calcareous ground. Seedlings establish more readily than many older sainfoin selections, but the stand still benefits from a clean, firm seedbed and freedom from weed competition in the first season. Because it is intolerant of wet or acid soils, reserve it for alkaline, low-rainfall range and pasture sites rather than heavy or waterlogged ground.

common_name: Endura Kura Clover (Improved-Vigor Rhizomatous Pasture Legume)

planting.note: Scarify and inoculate seed with the specific kura-clover rhizobium strain before drilling shallowly into a firm, weed-free seedbed; Endura was selected at the University of Minnesota for faster seedling establishment than older kura clover sources.

directions: Endura is a kura clover cultivar released through University of Minnesota forage breeding work aimed at overcoming the notoriously slow establishment that has limited kura clover's use in pastures and living mulches. Like other kura clovers it spreads by rhizomes into a dense, long-lived sod rather than relying on reseeding, so give it a full season or more with light mowing or grazing to suppress weeds while the rhizome network fills in. Once established it persists for many years under grazing, mowing, or no-till interseeding, fixing nitrogen steadily and tolerating both wet spells and short droughts better than white clover. Avoid tillage once stands are set, since the same rhizomatous habit that gives it persistence makes it slow to recover from soil disturbance.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Kura Clover for Pasture and Cover
